name: Photo comparison / flip test

lead: The flip test means comparing your photo with a horizontally flipped copy, or with your mirror image, to understand why you look different in pictures and which version looks better.

The chain: compare the versions, notice which side or look is more flattering, then choose angles and framing accordingly. Users say familiarity with the mirror image shapes preference, which relates to the mere-exposure effect, first studied by Zajonc in 1968. No studies have tested the practice itself.

paras: People flip selfies in a photo app, view them beside the originals and pick the version or angle they prefer for profiles and posts. It takes minutes and is often repeated across several photos.
No physical risks. Some community members report distress from close self-scrutiny.

chain: Spot which side or version looks better
angle.text: Users flip photos or compare them with their mirror image to understand why they look different in pictures and to pick the more flattering version and angle. It relates to the mere-exposure effect, though the method itself has not been tested.

lead: The photo comparison or flip test is a looksmaxxing practice in which a person compares photos of themselves with their mirror image, or flips a photo horizontally, to judge which version looks better or to understand why they look different in pictures than in the mirror.

No studies found directly testing the practice. Related psychology includes the mere-exposure effect, in which repeated exposure to a stimulus increases liking, first studied by Zajonc in 1968.[1] Reference works also describe facial symmetry as an attractiveness factor.[2]

paras: The mere-exposure effect holds that familiarity increases liking; Bornstein's 1989 meta-analysis of 208 experiments found r = 0.26.[1] Proponents of the flip test say people prefer their mirrored face because it is the one they see most. Wikipedia's mere-exposure page does not cover this specific claim, so the connection is the proponents' reasoning.[1]
Facial symmetry research is reported to link symmetry with perceived attractiveness, which is one reason communities compare original and flipped images.[2]

Community members use flips and side-by-side comparisons to evaluate symmetry, jaw and other features, and some say photos show how others see them. These views are not backed by published tests of the practice.
